routes.description: Defend libertarian agency by separating causal compulsion from non-causal determination, preserving sourcehood, and using Bradleyan idealism to resist naturalist exhaustion claims.
routes.successCriteria: Show that determinist description does not eliminate agential sourcehood and that idealism explains dimensions of experience omitted by reductive naturalism.

motionBridge.description: Libertarian freedom and Bradleyan idealism jointly withstand determinist and naturalist pressure better than a merely pragmatic reconstruction.

centralBridges.description: Mathematical determination does not by itself establish causal compulsion or eliminate agency.
Feeling, value, agency, and aesthetic experience exceed the scope of scientific representation.
Bradleyan inquiry culminates in an absolute integrating thought, feeling, value, and agency.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Practical distinctions between actions and bodily occurrences support treating agency as real.

routes.description: Maintain determinist pressure on libertarian alternatives while reconstructing freedom and idealism through their practical and experiential functions without Bradleyan metaphysical commitments.
routes.successCriteria: Show that libertarian alternatives remain inadequately secured and that pragmatic functional standards preserve responsibility and experiential priority more economically.

motionBridge.description: Compatibilist pragmatism answers the relevant pressures without requiring libertarian branching or a substantially real Bradleyan absolute.

centralBridges.description: Removing causal language does not itself restore genuine alternative futures.
Freedom remains socially indispensable as a distinction governing incentives, responsibility, and behavioral influence under determinism.
Experience can be treated as primary while physical objects remain useful models, without non-naturalistic ontology.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Anti-reductionist inquiry still needs practical standards that exclude arbitrary metaphysical additions.

sections.title: Agency and Laplacean Determinism
sections.rationale: This opening exchange establishes the affirmative datum of agency and the principal deterministic pressure that the later distinctions attempt to answer.

sections.title: Causal and Non-Causal Determination
sections.rationale: This exchange contains the affirmative's principal idealist distinction and the strongest immediate objection that non-causal fixity still threatens libertarian alternatives.

sections.title: Pragmatic Freedom and Metaphysical Agency
sections.rationale: This section captures the con side's positive compatibilist-pragmatist route and the affirmative's attempt to show that its practical distinctions presuppose real agency.

sections.title: Experiential Priority and Naturalized Idealism
sections.rationale: This exchange presents the Bradleyan foundation that reality exceeds rational representation and the con side's strongest accommodating alternative.

sections.title: Truth, Experience, and the Given
sections.rationale: This section tests the affirmative's idealist theory of truth against the objection that all accessible perception is already cognitively structured.

sections.title: The Absolute or a Regulative Ideal
sections.rationale: The final decisive exchange tests whether Bradley's absolute is justified as real or functions only as an aspirational endpoint of inquiry.
